clue.text: The Fairy King in Borneo resort (6)

indicators.note: Heard as re-sort, the word is an instruction to sort the letters again into a different order.

blocks.note: the six letters of the island's name, which is all the fodder there is

explanation.surface: A fairy monarch taking a holiday at a beach resort in Borneo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' arrives dressed as the place you fly to and is doing duty as a verb. The first half of the clue reads as one continuous phrase about a king abroad, which hides where the definition stops.
explanation.definitionFit: Oberon rules the fairy court in A Midsummer Night's Dream and in the medieval romances behind it, so the title names him directly.

clue.text: Dirty money’s source, concerning fraud in sports equipment (9,6)

blocks.note: dirty dealing and bad dealing are the same thing
a mint is the works where coins are struck, so money comes from one
a book on birds is a book concerning birds
a racket is a dishonest scheme run for money

explanation.surface: A trail from laundered cash to a swindle being run through sports gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Money's source' is not a rich relative but the building where coins are struck. Badminton takes its name from Badminton House in Gloucestershire, where the game was first played in the 1860s.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Sports equipment' places it by category: the strung frame a player swings at a shuttlecock is the kit that game needs.

clue.text: Burmese city developed ladders? Tell me more (7)

blocks.note: a stocking that has developed ladders has run
'Go on' is what you say to keep somebody talking, and its two words run together

explanation.surface: Gossip about a Burmese city, with the listener pressing for the rest of it.
explanation.walkthrough: A ladder in British English is the run that opens up a stocking or a pair of tights, which is the verb the first chunk wants. Three words of the clue turn into two, with the join between them moved.
explanation.definitionFit: Rangoon is the colonial-era name of Yangon, the river port that served as Burma's capital until 2006, so the definition places it by country.

clue.text: Bedtime booze coming – drop of tequila – tops! (9)

indicators.note: A drop of something is the smallest part of it you can take, which from a word is its opening letter.

blocks.note: what is nigh is close at hand, the sense in 'the end is nigh'
the letter the spirit starts on, as the instruction in front asks
caps are what go on top of bottles

explanation.surface: A drinks trolley on its way over, a splash of tequila included, and everyone delighted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tops!' reads as a cry of approval and is a plain noun instead. The three dashes chop the clue into fragments that look like separate exclamations, which is what keeps the pieces from lining up on the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightcap is the last drink taken before bed, named after the woollen cap people once wore to sleep in.

clue.text: Craving for drink, son moves eastward in short-sleeved top (6)

indicators.note: S is the standard letter for son, and sending it eastward slides it rightwards through the word named next, leaving that word's letters in a new order.

blocks.note: a T-shirt is the short-sleeved top, and its six letters are the ones in play

explanation.surface: A boy heading east in nothing but a T-shirt, desperate for something to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The instruction is unusually precise for an anagram: one named letter is moved and everything else keeps its place. Reading 'T-shirt' as six letters rather than as a garment is the step that unlocks it.
explanation.definitionFit: Thirst is the dry want that sends you looking for a glass of something, so a craving for drink is what the noun names.

clue.text: Infant happy to count (3,2)

blocks.note: a tot is a small child
somebody in good spirits is up, the opposite of down

explanation.surface: A cheerful baby old enough to start counting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Happy' looks like it is describing the infant and is a separate piece, standing in for a two-letter word meaning elated. 'To' is the only join here and carries no letters of its own.
explanation.definitionFit: To tot up a column of figures is to add them together, which is what counting a set of things amounts to.

clue.text: Decorate cake – younger Scout getting lemonade finally – what keeps it cool? (3,4)

indicators.note: What comes finally comes last, so the word in front of it gives up only the letter it ends on.

blocks.note: to ice a cake is to cover it in a sugar coating
a Cub is a member of the junior branch of the British Scouts, roughly eight to ten years old
the letter this word finishes on

explanation.surface: Icing a cake at a party while a small Scout gets through the last of the lemonade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decorate cake' wants a verb, not the noun that sits on top of one. The question mark on the definition is an admission that 'it' has deliberately been left unsaid.
explanation.definitionFit: An ice cube is the frozen block dropped into a glass to chill what is in it, so the definition names it by its only job.

clue.text: Keeps thick jeans out for cold-weather clothing (9,6)

indicators.note: Something put out is put out of order, so the letters named in front of it no longer stand as they were given.

blocks.note: fifteen letters of fodder, the full depth of the grid

explanation.surface: A wardrobe that shuts out the heavy denim in favour of something warmer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeps … out' reads as one phrasal verb with the jeans sitting inside it, and only its last word is the instruction. Fifteen letters is the whole depth of the grid, so the enumeration alone shows where the fodder has to end.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheepskin jacket is cut from fleece-lined hide and worn for warmth, so the definition names it by the season it is bought for.

clue.text: Advice regarding no-fly zone? Let’s change subject (4,2,5)

blocks.note: the one sensible thing to tell a pilot about airspace he is barred from entering
the modern brush-off for a topic somebody would rather not have opened

explanation.surface: A pilot being warned off restricted airspace, then steering the conversation elsewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: A no-fly zone is airspace aircraft are barred from, so the advice about one is meant literally. The same three words are modern slang for shutting a topic down, and the question mark is the setter admitting the first reading is a definition by situation.
explanation.definitionFit: The advice about a barred patch of sky is simply to keep out of it, and the same phrase is what you say to close an unwelcome subject off.

clue.text: Desist from throwing up cooking vessels (4)

indicators.note: In a down entry the letters run downwards, so a piece thrown up is read back from its foot to its head.

blocks.note: pots are the vessels you cook in, and sent up the column those four letters arrive this way round

explanation.surface: Somebody being told to quit hurling the saucepans about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throwing up' looks like nausea in a kitchen and is only a direction of travel: in a down entry, upward means read from the foot of the column back.
explanation.definitionFit: To desist is to leave off doing something, which is the plain imperative sense of the answer.

clue.text: Bean containers rejected in a mood (4)

indicators.note: Something rejected is thrown back, so the letters named come out running the other way.

blocks.note: beans come in tins, and thrown back up the column those four letters read this way

explanation.surface: Tins of beans sent back by a shopper in a temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected' is the setter asking for a turnaround, not a customer returning the groceries. In Britain baked beans come in tins rather than cans, which is the word the clue is quietly after.
explanation.definitionFit: A snit is a brief huff of bad temper, the low-level sulk that 'a mood' names in everyday speech.

clue.text: Not hip, not fancy – and balding (4,2,3)

indicators.note: Something fancy has been worked over into a more elaborate shape, and letters worked over do not keep the order they came in.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, the comma between them only punctuation

explanation.surface: A brisk verdict on a man who is unfashionable, unshowy and losing his hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not fancy' reads as a single phrase and has to be split, with the second 'not' joining the letters and 'fancy' turned into the instruction. A setter can use 'not' this way precisely because the eye reads it as attached to whatever follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair going from the crown outwards is described this way in British English, a gentler phrase for the state 'balding' names bluntly.

clue.text: Peacekeepers write: ‘Release from enclosure!’ (5)

blocks.note: the United Nations, whose blue-helmeted soldiers are the peacekeepers
to pen something is to write it

explanation.surface: United Nations staff putting a demand for somebody's release in writing.
explanation.walkthrough: UN for the United Nations is one of the most-used two-letter pieces in the game, and 'peacekeepers' is its usual disguise. The exclamation mark serves the surface's shouted demand and changes nothing about the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The un- prefix undoes what follows it, so opening the enclosure and letting the animals out is exactly the reverse of shutting them in.

clue.text: Favourite – Oxford, perhaps – with a flower (7)

blocks.note: a pet subject is a favourite one
Oxford is one university among many, and uni is the British short form
used literally

explanation.surface: Somebody's favourite, an Oxford man perhaps, turning up with a bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oxford, perhaps' flags a definition by example — that 'perhaps' is the setter's signal that one particular thing is standing in for the general class. Uni is what British students call the place; Americans say college.
explanation.definitionFit: The petunia is the trumpet-flowered bedding plant that fills summer window boxes, so 'flower' names it by kind.

clue.text: How Spooner introduces Hancock to Starmer: a little furry creature (7)

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner's trademark slip was to exchange the opening sounds of two words as he said them, so the pair of names spoken here trade their fronts.

blocks.note: Keir Starmer leads the Labour Party and is Britain's prime minister; his first name gives up its k and takes the m from the other
Matt Hancock was the health secretary through Britain's Covid lockdowns; his first name gives up its m and takes the k

explanation.surface: Spooner performing an introduction between two politicians and mangling it.
explanation.walkthrough: Introducing one person to another means addressing the second of them first, so the names come out in the order Starmer, Hancock — the reverse of how the clue lists them. Spooner was an Oxford don whose tongue-slips gave the device its name.
explanation.definitionFit: A meerkat is the small mongoose of the southern African deserts that stands upright on sentry duty, so the definition fits it by size and coat.

clue.text: Mechanic’s nasty accident (9)

indicators.note: Something nasty has been mistreated, and letters mistreated come out in a different order from the one they were handed over in.

blocks.note: the eight letters of the word plus the s after its apostrophe

explanation.surface: A car mechanic involved in an unpleasant smash.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe reads as a possessive and is simply another letter of the fodder, which is the whole of the disguise. A three-word clue leaves nowhere for a definition to hide except at one end or the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A mischance is a piece of bad luck or a mishap, which is what 'accident' means when nobody is to blame for it.

clue.text: Guilty! Eve naughtily eats, satisfying insidious serpent – in the beginning? (7)

definitions.text: Guilty! Eve naughtily eats, satisfying insidious serpent – in the beginning?

indicators.note: What stands in the beginning of a word is the letter it opens on, so each word of the list gives up just that one.

blocks.note: the opening letter of the first word
the first letter of the woman's name
the opening letter of the adverb
the letter this verb begins with
the letter at the head of this one
the opening letter of the serpent's adjective
the first letter of the last word before the dash

explanation.surface: The garden of Eden: Eve taking the fruit, with the serpent pleased at what it has set going.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash marks where the letters stop and the closing phrase begins, yet that phrase belongs to the sentence as much as to the wordplay. 'In the beginning' is how the book itself opens, which is why it can do both jobs at once.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue tells the story of the Bible's first book — the woman, the serpent and the fruit, at the very start of everything.

clue.text: Shocked exclamation: Gee! Venomous reptile! (4)

blocks.note: the letter G written out as it is said
the asp is the small venomous snake of Egypt and North Africa

explanation.surface: Someone crying out at the sight of a poisonous snake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gee!' is already a startled noise, so the surface uses it for the very job the definition names while the letters want only its spelling. The asp is the snake Cleopatra is said to have died by.
explanation.definitionFit: A gasp is the sharp indrawn breath of surprise, and set down on the page it serves as the cry of shock itself.

clue.text: What the competent come up to score (7)

definitions.text: What the competent come up to

blocks.clueFragment: What the competent come up to
blocks.note: the mark a person has to reach before being judged good enough
the verb for cutting a shallow line across a surface

explanation.surface: A capable player rising to the occasion and putting points on the board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come up to' belongs to the idiom in the first half rather than being an instruction to turn anything round, which is the thing to resist in a down entry. 'Score' looks like a tally of points and is wanted as a verb for cutting a groove.
explanation.definitionFit: To come up to scratch is to meet the mark boxers once had to toe at the start of a round; to scratch a surface is to score it.

clue.text: Word for word? (7)

blocks.note: read as the opening of the phrase meaning verbatim, and meant as the thing being asked for — a single word
read as the rest of that phrase, and meant as a job description: standing in place of another word

explanation.surface: A note that something has been repeated verbatim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Word for word' is a fixed phrase meaning exactly as spoken, and the whole trick is to read its middle preposition as 'in place of' instead. Three words is about as short as a cryptic definition gets, and the question mark is the only warning you are given.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym is one word offered in place of another of the same meaning, so the clue is literally a word for a word.

clue.text: What a patient needs is occasional sipping (7)

blocks.note: the care given to the sick, on a ward or at home
what somebody does to one glass they mean to make last the evening

explanation.surface: A hospital patient wanting care and taking the odd sip of water.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is the drinker's sense: making one glass last a whole evening by sipping at it now and then. Nothing between the halves marks the switch, since 'is' is a bare join.
explanation.definitionFit: Sick people need looking after, which is nursing; and to nurse a drink is to sip slowly at it rather than finish the thing.

clue.text: Everyman’s standing up with very loud resentment (4)

indicators.note: In a down entry the letters run downwards, so a piece standing up is read back from its foot to its head.

blocks.note: the setter calls himself Everyman, so Everyman's is I'm, and climbing the column those two letters arrive this way round
ff is fortissimo, the marking a composer writes for very loud

explanation.surface: Everyman on his feet, voicing his annoyance at the top of his lungs.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman refers to himself in his own clues, so 'Everyman's' is his way of writing I'm — a signature of this series. The apostrophe-s is a letter of the answer, not punctuation.
explanation.definitionFit: A miff is a small huff of annoyance, resentment at its mildest rather than a lasting grudge.

clue.text: Step one – to be embraced by celebrity (5)

indicators.note: Something embraced is held on both sides, so the piece just named goes inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: a celebrity is a star
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A plan whose first instruction is to get a famous name to take you up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Step one' reads as the first item on a list and has to come apart: 'Step' is the definition and 'one' is a letter. The dash is placed to keep those two words looking like a pair.
explanation.definitionFit: A stair is one of the treads in a flight, so the two words name the same thing you put a foot on.

clue.text: Hubby explaining what happens after teams change ends? (5,4)

definitions.text: what happens after teams change ends?

blocks.note: the husband, as a wife might refer to him

blocks.clueFragment: what happens after teams change ends?
blocks.note: the part of a football or rugby match left to play once the sides have swapped over

explanation.surface: A husband holding forth about the second period of a football match.
explanation.walkthrough: Teams change ends at the interval of a football or rugby match, so what follows is the part still to be played. 'Hubby' is affectionate British slang for a husband, and the phrase it defines serves equally for a wife.
explanation.definitionFit: Your other half is your spouse, hubby included; and once the teams have swapped ends it is the other half of the match being played out.

clue.text: Darts players’ limits discovered in Rochester (5)

indicators.note: What is discovered in something was already sitting there, so the letters are read out of the word that follows without being moved.

blocks.note: five letters running unbroken through the middle of the city's name

explanation.surface: Darts players finding out how far back they must stand, somewhere in Rochester.
explanation.walkthrough: Rochester is a cathedral city in Kent, and the surface leaves you picturing a pub team there rather than reading the name for what is buried inside it. Only the first letter and the last go unused.
explanation.definitionFit: The oche, said 'ocky', is the raised line a darts player must stand behind to throw, so it is literally the limit of where they may go.

clue.text: Ink in sketch representing where to find washers (7,4)

indicators.note: To represent something is to present it again in another form, and letters presented again come out in a new arrangement.

blocks.note: eleven letters of fodder, with 'in' contributing two of them

explanation.surface: Ink used on a drawing that shows where the washers are kept.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Washers' is the trap: the surface offers the flat metal rings out of a toolbox, and the definition means the people and machines that do the washing up. 'In' looks like a link word and is two letters of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Washing up is done at the kitchen sink, so that is where washers — the ones with hands or a motor — are to be found.

clue.text: Cuts some sweet chestnuts (6)

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for a part of what follows rather than the whole of it, and that part is a run of letters standing together.

blocks.note: six letters bridging the gap, running from the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: Slicing into a handful of sweet chestnuts.
explanation.walkthrough: The buried run straddles the word break, which is where these are hardest to see. Sweet chestnuts are the edible ones roasted on British streets at Christmas, as opposed to the horse chestnut that gives children conkers.
explanation.definitionFit: To etch is to bite a line into metal or glass with acid or a needle, which is cutting into a surface.

clue.text: According to Cockney, Caribbean country’s having decentish innings? (6)

indicators.note: A Cockney is a Londoner from the East End, and that accent drops the h at the front of a word, so only the sound of what is left survives.

blocks.note: Haiti is the Caribbean country, and with its aitch dropped what you hear is a number

explanation.surface: A West Indian batsman putting together a respectable score, as a Londoner would tell it.
explanation.walkthrough: Haiti is said 'hay-tee', and it is the aitch at the front that the accent removes. The country shares the island of Hispaniola with the Dominican Republic and plays no cricket at all, which is what keeps the surface's innings looking Caribbean.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket an eighty is a good but not enormous individual score — applauded on the way off, yet short of the hundred that makes a headline.
